query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Directional solidification that aligns dual-phase lamellar colonies along the tensile axis will reduce misoriented interphase boundaries responsible for microcrack initiation, thereby simultaneously enhancing both room-temperature tensile strength and ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloys with dual-phase lamellar colonies produced via conventional casting, featuring randomly oriented internal boundaries that promote microcrack initiation during room-temperature deformation.
generation.intervention: Employ directional solidification with a carefully controlled thermal gradient and solidification front velocity to preferentially align the lamellar colonies along the tensile loading direction.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation tests on alloys of identical composition processed by directional solidification versus conventional casting.
generation.structural_mediator: Aligned lamellar colonies that present fewer misoriented interphase boundaries acting as stress concentrators.
generation.mechanism: By controlling the thermal gradient during solidification, the lamellar colonies become aligned with the tensile direction, decreasing the occurrence of unfavorable boundary orientations. This alignment minimizes local stress concentrations and microcrack nucleation while preserving the fine lamellar spacing that contributes to high strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The directionally solidified alloy is expected to exhibit both higher tensile strength and increased ductility, with a measurable reduction in microcrack density compared to the conventional lamellar microstructure.
generation.baseline: The conventional processing route producing eutectic alloys with randomly oriented lamellar colonies and a high density of misaligned internal boundaries.
generation.boundary: The benefits of this intervention are expected within a specific range of controlled solidification parameters; deviations in alloy composition or processing conditions outside these parameters may not yield improved properties.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the improvements in strength and ductility is uncertain and likely dependent on the optimization of directional solidification parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the same eutectic high-entropy alloy composition: one set processed by conventional casting and the other set by directional solidification under controlled thermal gradient conditions. Perform room-temperature tensile tests with in-situ microstructural observation (e.g., using high-resolution electron microscopy) to assess lamellar colony alignment and microcrack formation.
measurements: Microcrack initiation and propagation via microscopic imaging
Degree of lamellar colony alignment via quantitative microstructural analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the directionally solidified samples do not show statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility, or if microcrack density is not reduced relative to the conventionally processed samples.

decision.trend: Early work on eutectic high-entropy alloys – as exemplified by PMC4145285 – focused on producing fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructures via conventional casting and modest cold rolling. These treatments increased strength but, by creating a high density of randomly oriented interlamellar boundaries, they also promoted microcrack nucleation under room-temperature tension, thus sacrificing ductility. Later studies explored varied thermo‐mechanical treatments, microstructural design (e.g., precipitate engineering), and even directional solidification in other HEA systems. Although these interventions improved one property or another, they did not resolve the inherent brittleness associated with misaligned, dual-phase lamellar colonies.
decision.unsolved: The core limitation remains the trade-off between strength and ductility: the randomly oriented internal boundaries in the dual-phase lamellar colonies act as stress concentrators that trigger microcracking, leaving room-temperature tensile ductility far below acceptable levels without undermining strength.
decision.lever: Employ directional solidification with a carefully controlled thermal gradient and solidification front velocity to preferentially align the lamellar colonies along the tensile loading direction
decision.why: Aligning the lamellar colonies is hypothesized to reduce the incidence of detrimental, misoriented interphase boundaries that serve as microcrack nucleation sites. This processing intervention builds on prior trends—where adjustments in processing influenced microstructure yet failed to overcome brittleness—and offers a targeted route to simultaneously enhance strength (via retained fine lamellar spacing) and ductility (by minimizing stress concentrations at boundaries). The experiment could compare room-temperature tensile properties of directionally solidified specimens versus conventionally cast ones; a lack of improvement or an increase in microcrack formation would falsify the hypothesis.
